text.p: Bezeq Israel Telecom's board on Thursday named Ami Erel managing director, Bezeq said.
The announcement came as Israel's ministerial privatisation committee on Thursday approved a plan to sell 25 percent of Bezeq, reducing its holding to 51 percent by the end of the year.
Erel, 50, an electronics engineer by training, was for the last seven years the secretary-general of the Idan-Elitec group. Idan provides telecommunications services and products.

He takes over from acting managing director Avi Hochman who filled the spot when a civil service watchdog committee refused to let Yoram Turbowicz take the job until he sat out a one-year cooling-off period because of a possible conflict of interest.
Turbowicz had been due to take over the managing director's job from Yitzhak Kaul on March 2. He subsequently said he would not accept the post.

Bezeq, Israel's main telecommunication carrier, has seen its monopoly over telecommunications service gradually whittled down over the years, but it retains monopolies in basic service and infrastructure.

Moshe Leon, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's chief economics adviser, said on Thursday the plan to sell 25 percent of Bezeq called for selling some of the shares -- probably 10 percent -- through a public offering in the Israeli capital market.
The rest would be sold by other means yet to be determined, he said.
Leon told Reuters that the domestic public flotation would be in another two to three months. He declined to speculate on how the remaining shares would be sold.
The Israeli government currently holds 76 percent of Bezeq. The rest trades on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, although about half the float is controlled by Britain's Cable and Wireless PLC.
Israel has been in lengthy negotiations with Cable and Wireless over the British company's future role in Bezeq, but officials said no agreement had yet been reached.

Communications Minister Limor Livnat and other officials have been pushing hard to speed the privatisation of Bezeq. Shares in the company were originally supposed to be floated in a global offering, but in February she approved a plan for a domestic offering on the grounds it could be done more quickly.

Government sources said they hoped they could raise about $500 million from the sale of the 25 percent stake. Bezeq's market capitalisation is currently $1.9 billion. Part of the proceeds might go to the company itself, they added.

Bezeq officials have said they prefer a global offering, which would raise the company's profile in international financial markets. In addition, the weakness of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange precludes floating all the shares domestically, officials have said.
